name: Percentages
intro: **Name the base before you compute.** Almost every wrong answer in this topic is a right calculation on the wrong base (§3).
Work in multiplying factors, not in additions: +25% is ×5/4, −20% is ×4/5. Chains then collapse in one line (§5).

qs.h: §2 — 37.5% is 3/8. Never long-multiply by 0.375.

qs.q: If 15% of a number is 45, then 40% of the same number is
qs.h: §1 — find the number first, or scale directly: 40/15 = 8/3.

qs.q: What percentage of 250 is 45?
qs.h: §3 — "of 250" names the base. It goes in the denominator.

qs.q: 62.5% of 800 equals
A number increased by 25% gives 350. Find the original number.
qs.h: §3 — divide by 1.25, don't subtract 25% of 350. The base is the original, not the result.

qs.q: If A is 300 and B is 240, then B is less than A by
qs.h: §3 — "less than A" makes A the base, so divide by 300, not 240.
qs.s: 60/300 = 20%. (Dividing by 240 gives 25% — that would answer "A is more than B by …".)

qs.q: If A is 25% more than B, then B is less than A by
qs.h: §4 — 25% is 1/4 more, so the reverse is 1/5 less.
qs.s: A : B = 5 : 4 ⟹ B is short by 1 part out of 5 = 20%.

qs.q: If A's income is 33.33% more than B's, by what percent is B's income less than A's?
qs.h: §4 table — 1/3 more corresponds to 1/4 less.
qs.s: A : B = 4 : 3 ⟹ B is short by 1 part out of 4 = 25%.

qs.q: If the price of sugar is 20% less than that of rice, the price of rice is more than that of sugar by
qs.h: §4 — 1/5 less reverses to 1/4 more.
qs.s: Sugar : rice = 4 : 5 ⟹ rice exceeds sugar by 1/4 = 25%.

qs.q: A's salary is 20% less than B's. By what percent is B's salary more than A's?
qs.h: §4 — same pair as B3, stated the other way round.
qs.s: A : B = 4 : 5 ⟹ B exceeds A by 1/4 = 25%.

qs.q: If X is 60% of Y, then Y exceeds X by
qs.h: §4 — the base flips from Y to X. Y/X = 5/3.
qs.s: X : Y = 3 : 5 ⟹ Y exceeds X by 2/3 = 66.67%. (40% answers "X is less than Y by …".)

qs.q: The price of an article rises 20% and then falls 20%. Find the net percentage change (enter a negative number for a fall).
qs.h: §5 — chain the factors. Equal up-then-down percentages never cancel.

qs.q: A salary is increased by 25% and then decreased by 20%. The net change is
qs.h: §5 — 5/4 × 4/5. The fractions are reciprocals, which is exactly why this pair does cancel.
qs.s: 1.25 × 0.8 = 1 ⟹ no change. Contrast C1: it is the fractions, not the percentages, that must be reciprocal.

qs.q: A town's population rises 10% in the first year, 20% in the second and 25% in the third, reaching 33,000. Find the population 3 years ago.
qs.h: §6 — chain the three factors, then divide. Do not subtract 55%.

qs.q: The length of a rectangle increases by 20% and the breadth decreases by 10%. The area changes by
qs.h: §5 — area is a product, so multiply the factors. The naive +20 − 10 = +10 is planted.

qs.q: A quantity is increased by 30% and then increased by 30% again. Find the total percentage increase.
After two successive discounts of 10% and 20%, an article sells for ₹1,440. Its marked price was
qs.h: §5 — the combined factor is 0.72, not 0.70. Then divide.
qs.s: 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72 ⟹ MP = 1440/0.72 = ₹2,000. (Using a single 30% discount gives ₹2,057 — not an option, which is your check.)

qs.q: The price of petrol rises 25%. By what percent must consumption be reduced to keep expenditure unchanged?
qs.h: §7 — expenditure = price × consumption, so the two factors must be reciprocal. 25% up is 1/4; the cut is 1/5.
qs.s: New consumption factor = 1/1.25 = 0.8 ⟹ reduction = 20%. (Answering 25% is the standard error.)

qs.q: The price of rice falls 20%. By what percent can a family increase consumption without increasing expenditure?
qs.h: §7 in the other direction — 1/0.8.

qs.q: The price of sugar rises from ₹30/kg to ₹36/kg. By what percent must a family reduce consumption so that expenditure rises by only 10%? Give the answer to two decimals.
qs.h: §7, generalised — the consumption factor is (target expenditure factor)/(price factor).
qs.s: Price factor 1.2, expenditure factor 1.1 ⟹ consumption factor = 1.1/1.2 = 11/12 ⟹ reduction = 1/12 = 8.33%.

qs.q: A man's salary rises 20% and his expenditure rises 10%. If his savings were 20% of his salary, his savings rise by
qs.h: §1 — assume a salary of 100, tabulate before and after. Savings are a residue, so they move much faster than either component.

qs.q: If the price of an article is reduced by 20%, a man can buy 5 kg more for ₹600. Find the original price per kg (in ₹).
qs.h: §7 — write the quantity at each price as 600/p and 600/0.8p, then take the difference.

sets.name: Percentage points, remainders and percentages of percentages

qs.q: A bank raises its interest rate from 4% to 5%. This is
qs.h: §8 — 1 percentage point is not 1%. The base for a percentage change is the old rate.
qs.s: 1/4 = a 25% increase (or equivalently, a rise of 1 percentage point).

qs.q: A man spends 30% of his income on rent and 20% of the remainder on food. What percentage of his income is left?
qs.h: §9 — "of the remainder" resets the base to what is left, not to the original.
qs.s: 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 ⟹ 56%. (Treating both as percentages of income gives 50% — the planted error.)

qs.q: In a school 60% of the students are boys, and 25% of the boys wear glasses. The percentage of the whole school that is boys wearing glasses is
qs.h: §12 — a percentage of a percentage is a product.

qs.q: A man spends 25% of his salary on rent, 30% of the remainder on food, and saves the rest, which is ₹5,250. Find his salary (in ₹).
qs.h: §9 — chain 0.75 and 0.70 to get the saved fraction, then divide.

qs.q: The pass percentage in an exam rose from 40% to 48%. Expressed as a percentage of the earlier figure, the increase is
qs.h: §8 — the rise is 8 percentage points; the question asks for the relative change.

qs.q: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 60% of the votes and won by 1,200 votes. Find the total number of votes polled.
qs.h: §10 — the margin is 60 − 40 = 20 percentage points of the total.

qs.q: A student scores 30% and fails by 30 marks. Another scores 45% and gets 15 marks more than the pass mark. The maximum marks are
qs.h: §10 — the gap between the two scores is 45 marks and 15 percentage points. Subtract the two equations.

qs.q: A candidate needs 40% to pass. He scores 160 marks and fails by 40 marks. Find the maximum marks.
qs.h: §10 — the pass mark is what he scored plus what he was short by.

qs.q: In an election, 20% of the registered voters did not vote. The winner got 60% of the votes cast and won by 3,200 votes. The number of registered voters is
qs.h: §10 — two bases here: the margin is a percentage of the votes cast, which is itself a percentage of the registered voters.
qs.s: Margin = 20% of votes cast = 0.20 × 0.80V = 0.16V = 3200 ⟹ V = 20,000. (Ignoring the turnout gives 16,000 — an option.)

qs.q: In an exam, 35% failed in Maths, 45% failed in English and 20% failed in both. What percentage passed in both subjects?
qs.h: §10 — inclusion–exclusion for those who failed at least one, then take the complement.
qs.s: Failed at least one = 35 + 45 − 20 = 60% ⟹ passed both = 40%.

qs.q: In an election among three candidates, A got 45% and B got 35% of the votes. If C got 4,000 votes, the total number of votes was
qs.h: §10 — C's share is the residue.

qs.q: If the price of a commodity increases by 60%, by what percent must consumption be reduced to keep expenditure unchanged?
qs.h: Reciprocal of 1.6.

qs.q: Find 40% of 60% of 250.
qs.h: Multiply the factors.

qs.q: A number is increased by 20% and the result is then decreased by 25%. The net change is
A man's income rises 25% while his tax rate falls from 20% to 16%. Find the percentage change in the tax he pays (enter 0 if unchanged).
qs.h: Tax = income × rate, so chain the two factors.

qs.q: If A's salary is 20% more than B's, and B's is 25% more than C's, then A's salary exceeds C's by
qs.h: Chain 6/5 and 5/4.

qs.q: A salary is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. If the final salary is ₹19,200, find the original salary (in ₹).
qs.h: The net factor is 0.96.

qs.q: In a class of 50, 40% are girls. If 10 more girls join, the percentage of girls becomes
qs.h: The denominator changes too.
qs.s: Girls 20, boys 30. After: 30 girls out of 60 = 50%. (Forgetting to update the total gives 60%.)

qs.q: A shopkeeper reduces the price of an item by 20%, which increases sales volume by 30%. Find the percentage change in revenue.
qs.h: Revenue is a product of price and quantity.

qs.q: A man spends 75% of his income. If his income rises 20% and his expenditure rises 10%, his savings rise by
qs.h: Assume 100 and tabulate.

qs.q: In an exam a candidate scoring 25% fails by 30 marks, while one scoring 50% gets 20 marks more than the pass mark. Find the pass mark.
qs.h: Subtract the two statements to get the maximum first, then back out the pass mark.

audit: computing on the wrong base — the phrase "of" or "than" always names it (§3)
B1–B5
reversing a percentage comparison by reusing the same number instead of the reciprocal fraction (§4)
adding successive percentage changes instead of multiplying the factors (§5)
C2
assuming equal percentages never cancel — they do when the fractions are reciprocal
subtracting the total percentage from the final value instead of dividing by the chained factor
quoting the price change as the consumption change — they are reciprocal, never equal (§7)
D4, M9
computing on income or expenditure instead of on savings, which is a residue and moves fastest
E1, E5
confusing percentage points with a percentage change (§8)
E2, E4
applying the second percentage to the original rather than to the remainder (§9)
F1, F4
forgetting that the winning margin is the difference of the shares, and that turnout is a second base (§10)
solving one equation at a time instead of subtracting to eliminate the pass mark
M7
changing the numerator but not the denominator
